extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (discrete math / intro proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and solution-style expectations for writing and checking elementary proofs in logic, set theory, relations, and functions (typical undergraduate/discrete-math exercises). Emphasizes element-chasing, quantifier manipulation, case analysis, existence/uniqueness, and standard relation/function arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical equivalences for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by showing that ∃x(P(x) ∨ Q(x)) is equivalent to ¬∀x¬(P(x) ∨ Q(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply De Morgan's laws and quantifier negation to rewrite existential statements as negated universals (and vice versa) in order to simplify or re-express formulas for use in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set inclusion/equality by element-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show e.g. (∀x∈A P(x)) ∧ (∀x∈B P(x)) ⇔ ∀x∈(A∪B) P(x), rewrite hypotheses as universal implications and work with an arbitrary element x to derive membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let x be arbitrary, expand definitions (x∈A → P(x)), rewrite implications as disjunctions if helpful, and show left-to-right and right-to-left containments separately to establish equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert set nonexistence to subset statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A \ B = ∅ is equivalent to ¬∃x(x∈A ∧ x∉B) which is equivalent to ∀x(x∉A ∨ x∈B) and hence to ∀x(x∈A → x∈B) and thus to A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain the logical equivalences (negation of existential → universal of negation → implication) to turn emptiness claims into subset relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential and universal instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof uses ∃x φ(x), choose a particular witness x0 with φ(x0). When a premise is ∀x φ(x), you may instantiate φ for an arbitrary or particular element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply existential instantiation to get a concrete witness and universal instantiation to apply universal facts to the chosen element; be explicit about which variable is chosen and why it satisfies needed properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose c ≤ d. ... (use ¬Q → ¬P instead of P → Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving an implication P→Q, it may be clearer to assume ¬Q and prove ¬P. State explicitly that you are proving the contrapositive and then proceed with the assumed negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired conclusion and derive a contradiction (e.g., assume A ⊆ B\C but A and C are not disjoint and derive conflicting membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by supposing the opposite of what you want to prove, use the hypotheses to derive an impossibility (x and not x), then conclude the original statement must hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis (proof by cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the argument into exhaustive cases (e.g., x∈B vs x∉B; x−4≥0 vs x−4<0) and prove the claim in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the cases cover all possibilities and treat each case separately; subcases are allowed. After handling all cases, conclude the overall statement holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce an arbitrary element to prove universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x be arbitrary. Then show the required property for that x to conclude a universal statement (∀x ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state that x is arbitrary, derive the property using given hypotheses, and then generalize to all x by the arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs by explicit construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x with a property, construct a witness (e.g., let y = x/(x^2 + 1) or let y = 2x) and verify it satisfies the desired equation/property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the explicit formula or element, show it is well-defined (denominators nonzero etc.), and verify the required property holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs: show any two witnesses are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness, assume two objects satisfy the property and deduce they are equal (e.g., suppose y and y' both satisfy an equation; pick a test value to force equality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard pattern: assume y1 and y2 have the property, manipulate equalities to derive y1 = y2, thereby establishing uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier order matters; introduce variables in correct sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the logical form, introduce variables in the correct order (e.g., for ∃x ∀y ... introduce x first, then y). You cannot define x in terms of y if y is introduced later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an outline indicates 'Let x = ... Let y be arbitrary', ensure definitions do not depend on later-introduced variables; if the order is wrong, the proof structure fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional proofs: prove both directions separately
rubrics_metrics.description: For a statement of the form A ⇔ B, prove A→B and B→A separately (e.g., ∀x(P∧Q) ⇔ (∀xP ∧ ∀xQ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each implication as its own proof, often using 'let x be arbitrary' for universal directions and constructing or deconstructing conjunctions as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to disprove universal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Show a concrete counterexample (explicit sets/numbers) to demonstrate a proposed theorem is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick small/simple examples that satisfy hypotheses but violate the conclusion; present them explicitly and check the violated property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate set-language to logical symbols and apply instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Write statements like 'F⊆G' or 'x∈∪F' in logical notation to see universal/existential structure and then apply existential or universal instantiation as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converting to quantifiers clarifies which hypotheses are universal and which are existential, guiding the use of instantiation steps in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite implications as disjunctions when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the equivalence (A → B) ≡ (¬A ∨ B) to transform implications (e.g., (x∈A → P(x)) ≡ (x∉A ∨ P(x))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can simplify logical manipulation inside universal quantifiers and make distribution/combination of clauses more straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle absolute-value and sign-dependent inequalities via case split
rubrics_metrics.description: For |x−4|, consider x−4≥0 and x−4<0 separately to manipulate absolute values into linear inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break into the two sign cases of the inner expression and proceed algebraically in each case (as shown for proving |2x−6| > x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove relation properties by checking the defining element-pair conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity, take arbitrary appropriate element(s)/pairs and verify the relation holds according to the definition (e.g., if R is reflexive, (x,x)∈R for all x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly apply the definitions on arbitrary elements or pairs; use closure operations (inverse, composition) and previously proven properties to deduce the desired features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish closure minimality by subset arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a closure (reflexive/symmetric/transitive closure) is the smallest relation with a property, prove R ⊆ S and that any other T with the property and containing R must also contain S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show S has the property and R⊆S; then assume T has the property and R⊆T and prove S⊆T by the minimality construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove injectivity/surjectivity using algebraic manipulations or constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Show one-to-one by assuming f(x1)=f(x2) and deducing x1=x2 via algebra; show onto by, given y, constructing x with f(x)=y (e.g., invert formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit algebraic rearrangements or inverse-like constructions; check domains/codomains to ensure constructed x is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show nonemptiness of composition via domain-range intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: S◦R ≠ ∅ iff Ran(R) and Dom(S) are not disjoint; to prove, produce the linking element b with (a,b)∈R and (b,c)∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with existential statements: to prove nonemptiness choose or exhibit b in Ran(R)∩Dom(S); for emptiness, argue contrapositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use element-wise arguments for families of sets (unions/intersections)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove identities like ∪(F∩G) ⊆ (∪F)∩(∪G), choose A∈F∩G with x∈A and deduce x∈∪F and x∈∪G; reverse containment similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpack definitions of ∪F and ∩F (existential/universal over the family) and use chosen A∈F or arbitrary membership in families to finish proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check proofs for exhaustiveness and correct variable introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that all cases are considered and that variables are introduced before they are used (e.g., cannot define x in terms of y before y is introduced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for missing cases or order-of-introduction errors (the page flags specific incorrect sentences and explains why they fail). Amend proof structure to fix these defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-delta / neighborhood arguments for limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Given lim_{x→c} f(x)=L>0, pick ε=L and find δ so that 0<|x−c|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<L, which yields f(x)>0 in a punctured neighborhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition of limit: choose an appropriate ε>0 and find δ>0 satisfying the implication to establish positivity or other local properties of f near c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with equivalence classes and partitions via representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: To relate quotient sets and induced relations, pick representatives x and use [x]_R and [x]_S intersections to describe classes (e.g., [x]_T = [x]_R ∩ [x]_S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use membership equivalences (y∈[x]_T iff (y,x)∈T) and previously proven lemmas about representatives to move between partitions and relations.
